templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. Your {lead} asks you to begin a new task while you are finishing another task that is due soon. The two tasks cannot both be finished at the same time.

options.text: Briefly explain the deadline conflict and ask your {lead} which task should take priority.
options.why: The two requests compete for the same time. Your {lead} can clarify priority so you can make a realistic plan.

options.text: Try to complete both tasks at once without telling anyone about the conflict.
options.why: Splitting attention may reduce quality and leaves the deadline conflict unresolved.
options.misconception: Working on more things at once always saves time.

options.text: Ignore the new request and finish the earlier task without responding.
options.why: The new request may be more urgent, and not responding prevents your {lead} from helping set priorities.
options.misconception: The first task mentioned always has priority.

options.text: Choose the task you prefer and tell your {lead} after both deadlines pass.
options.why: Waiting can create avoidable missed deadlines. Raise the conflict before choosing so expectations can be set.
options.misconception: A worker should privately guess which request matters more.

templates.principle: When tasks conflict, make the time constraint visible and clarify priority before the conflict causes missed work.

review.notes: The scenario explicitly establishes a schedule conflict and identifies the lead as the person to clarify priorities.

templates.timing: Clarify the conflict before switching tasks.

templates.scenario: At the start of a busy shift at {workplace|a}, you have more tasks than time to finish them.
templates.prompt: Arrange these planning steps in the order you would do them.

steps.text: Write down every task that needs to be done today
Mark which tasks have deadlines or people waiting on them
Rank the tasks from most urgent and important to least
Begin working on the top-ranked task

precedence.why: You cannot judge deadlines for tasks you have not listed yet.
A fair ranking depends on knowing which tasks have deadlines or people waiting.
Starting before ranking risks spending your time on a task that could have waited.

templates.principle: Plan before you start: list the work, identify deadlines and dependencies, rank by urgency and importance, then begin with the top priority.

review.notes: A natural dependency chain; no policy or jurisdiction content.

templates.scenario: Your {lead} asked you to finish {task|the} before your shift ends in an hour. Halfway through, {coworker} asks you to help with an urgent {client} request that would take about thirty minutes. You cannot do both in the time left, and your {lead} is nearby on the floor.

options.text: Quickly tell your {lead} about both demands and ask which one should come first.
options.why: Your {lead} owns the priorities and can see the whole picture. A quick check keeps both people informed and lets the most important work get done first.

options.text: Help {coworker} right away because {client|a} is waiting, then finish your own work as soon as you can.
options.why: Helping is understandable, but you would be choosing priorities on your own while your {lead} expects {task|the} finished. A quick conversation would have kept everyone informed.
options.misconception: An urgent request automatically outranks an assigned task.

options.text: Finish {task|the} first as assigned and tell {coworker} to find someone else.
options.why: Sticking to the assignment without checking ignores a possibly urgent need and leaves your {lead} unaware that {client|a} is waiting.
options.misconception: An assigned task always outranks a coworker's request.

options.text: Try to do both by switching back and forth, and hope neither one suffers much.
options.why: Splitting your attention usually slows both jobs and raises the chance of mistakes. It also hides the real problem, which is that the time is not enough.
options.misconception: Doing everything at once is the most productive approach.

templates.principle: When priorities collide, do not decide silently: tell the person who sets priorities what the competing demands are and let them direct the order.

review.notes: Lead is stated to be nearby, so asking is realistic. Acceptable option is a defensible helping instinct that bypasses the person who owns priorities.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. The posted maintenance schedule calls for routine upkeep of {equipment|the} today, which you are trained to do. It is a busy day, and skipping the upkeep would save thirty minutes.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Do the scheduled upkeep, or tell your {lead} you cannot fit it in so it can be rescheduled.
options.why: Regular upkeep keeps equipment working and lasting longer. If time truly does not allow it, rescheduling openly keeps it from being forgotten.

options.text: Skip it this once, since the equipment has been working fine and the day is unusually busy.
options.why: Equipment that seems fine today can fail sooner without upkeep. Skipping adds up, and a breakdown costs more time than thirty minutes.
options.misconception: If it works now, it does not need upkeep.

options.text: Do only part of the upkeep so that it takes less time, and mark the whole schedule item as done.
options.why: A partial job recorded as complete leaves the equipment under-maintained and the record inaccurate.

options.text: Put it off without telling anyone and plan to catch up on it whenever things settle down.
options.why: Unannounced delays are easy to forget, and others who rely on the schedule will assume it was done.
options.misconception: I can quietly reschedule things myself.

templates.principle: Look after equipment: do scheduled upkeep, or tell the person in charge so it can be rescheduled instead of skipped.

templates.scenario: Halfway through a shift at {workplace|the}, {coworker} calls out, and your {lead} asks you to cover {coworker}'s duties as well as your own. You now have more on your list than the time left allows.

options.text: Review your list for what is due today, and tell your {lead} which tasks may have to move.
options.why: Knowing what is urgent lets you protect the important work, and telling your {lead} early lets them adjust expectations.

options.text: Rush through every task at top speed and hope that the quality holds up on all of them.
options.why: Rushing everything raises the chance of errors and does not change the fact that there is not enough time. A plan comes first.
options.misconception: Working faster fixes any shortage of time.

options.text: Quietly drop the tasks you like least, and do not mention it unless someone asks.
options.why: Choosing by preference rather than by priority can leave important things undone, and others will be unaware of the gap.
options.misconception: I can choose which tasks to skip on my own.

options.text: Wait until the end of the shift to mention that some tasks were not finished, since you did your best.
options.why: Waiting leaves your {lead} no time to adjust, and people relying on those tasks will be surprised.
options.misconception: Reporting at the end is soon enough.

templates.principle: When the workload changes, prioritize by what is due, and tell your lead early which tasks may have to move.
templates.timing: The workload exceeds time; prioritizing and informing comes before any work.

templates.scenario: A coworker at {workplace|the} writes this plan for the morning.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is a problem.

segments.text: Plan for the morning, in the order I will work:
segments.whyFine: A heading that introduces the plan.

segments.text: 1. Reorganize the old supply shelf, which nobody is waiting on.
segments.why: Doing a task with no deadline first can crowd out tasks that are due, which makes the order a problem.

segments.text: 2. Send the reminder that goes out at 9:00.
segments.whyFine: A task with a set time is a priority.

segments.text: 3. Finish the report due at noon.
segments.whyFine: A task with a deadline is a priority.

templates.principle: Put tasks with deadlines or people waiting ahead of tasks that can wait.

review.notes: One line puts a no-deadline task ahead of timed ones.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and are finishing {task|the}, which includes clearing leftover items. Posted instructions show which items go in the recycling bin and which go in the trash. Sorting takes about two extra minutes.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Sort each item into the correct bin using the posted instructions.
options.why: Sorting waste the way the instructions show reduces what is thrown away and uses resources responsibly. Two minutes is a small cost for that.

options.text: Put everything in the trash to save time, since sorting makes little difference.
options.why: Small habits add up across a workplace. Following the guide keeps recyclable material out of the trash.
options.misconception: One person's sorting does not matter.

options.text: Leave the leftovers on the counter for the next shift, so that they can decide what to do.
options.why: Leaving the job unfinished creates extra work and mess for someone else, and does not follow the posted instructions.
options.misconception: Someone else can handle it later.

options.text: Take the recyclable items home to recycle them yourself, since you know how to do it better.
options.why: The workplace has a system for these items. Taking them home skips it and treats workplace property as your own.
options.misconception: Doing it my own way is more responsible.

templates.principle: Use resources responsibly by following posted guidance for sorting and disposing of waste.

review.notes: Posted guidance stated in scenario; no environmental regulation claims.
